_about.note: Single source of truth for the fundamental score thresholds AND the /learn page copy. services/fundamental_scoring.py grades against 'bands'; frontend/static/js/learn.js and the research-page info popovers render the prose. Edit a threshold here and both move together.
_about.verdicts: good | neutral | bad — these drive the colour shown in the UI. By default they award 1.0 / 0.55 / 0.10 of the metric weight.
_about.bands: Evaluated in order; the first band whose 'max' is >= the value wins. A band with max=null is the catch-all and must come last.
_about.points: Optional per-band override of the verdict's default award, between 0 and 1. Lets 'fairly valued' score below 'cheap' without needing a fourth verdict colour, so a genuinely excellent company reaches 100 and a merely solid one does not.

intro.title: Quality first, then price
intro.body: Work out whether it is a good business (ROE, ROCE, margins, cash flow). Only then ask whether the price is fair (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA). A wonderful business at a fair price beats a poor business at a cheap one.

intro.title: A ratio on its own means nothing
intro.body: Every number needs two comparisons: the same metric for rivals in the same industry, and the same company's own last five years. A P/E of 30 is cheap for an IT firm and expensive for a steel plant.

intro.title: One year is noise, three to five years is a trend
intro.body: A single great year can be a land sale, a tax refund, or a one-off order. Look at the direction across several years before believing any number.

intro.title: Cheap is not the same as good
intro.body: The most common beginner mistake is buying a low P/E on a business whose sales are shrinking. That is a value trap: the ratio is low because the market expects profits to fall.

intro.title: Fundamentals tell you what to buy, not when
intro.body: None of these numbers say anything about timing. That is what the Technical tab is for. A great company can still be a bad entry today.

intro.title: Check the source before you act
intro.body: This data comes from Yahoo Finance and for NSE tickers it can be stale, missing, or simply wrong. Before any real money moves, verify the figure in the company's own quarterly filing or on the NSE site.

valuation.label: Valuation
valuation.body: These ratios compare the share price to something real — profit, assets, or cash flow. They answer 'is this expensive?', never 'is this a good company?'.

profitability.label: Profitability
profitability.body: These measure how much profit the company squeezes out of the money and sales it has. This is where you find genuinely high-quality businesses.

balance_sheet.label: Balance sheet
balance_sheet.tagline: Can it survive a bad year
balance_sheet.body: Debt and cash. A profitable company with too much borrowing can still go under; a company sitting on net cash can ride out a downturn and buy rivals cheaply.

growth.label: Growth & ownership
growth.body: Sales and profit direction, plus how much of the company the founders still own. Growth justifies a high valuation — its absence makes a cheap stock a trap.

pe_ratio.label: P/E Ratio
pe_ratio.plain: How many years of the company's current profit you are paying for one share. A ₹2,400 share on a company earning ₹100 per share a year has a P/E of 24 — at today's profit it takes 24 years to earn your money back.

bands.note: Very cheap — check why the market is pessimistic
Expensive — needs strong growth to justify
Very expensive at this level of profit

pe_ratio.caveat: The sector decides what counts as normal: IT and branded FMCG routinely trade at 35–50, PSU banks at 6–12. A blank P/E means there was no profit to divide by.
pe_ratio.watch_out: A low P/E on a company whose revenue is falling is a value trap, not a bargain.

forward_pe.label: Forward P/E
forward_pe.formula: Share price ÷ next year's estimated earnings per share
forward_pe.plain: The same idea as P/E, but using what analysts think the company will earn next year instead of what it earned last year.
forward_pe.ideal: Lower than the trailing P/E — that means profits are expected to grow
forward_pe.caveat: This is a forecast, not a fact, and the forecasts are often wrong. It is shown for context and deliberately left out of the score.
forward_pe.watch_out: A forward P/E far below the trailing one can mean last year had a one-off gain that nobody expects to repeat.

pb_ratio.label: P/B Ratio
pb_ratio.formula: Share price ÷ book value per share (assets minus liabilities)
pb_ratio.plain: What you pay for ₹1 of the company's net assets — everything it owns minus everything it owes. A P/B of 3 means you are paying ₹3 for ₹1 of accounting net worth.

bands.note: Negative book value — liabilities exceed assets
Rich, unless the business is asset-light
Very high relative to net assets

pb_ratio.caveat: Nearly meaningless for IT and services companies — their value is people and contracts, not factories, so 10x book and above is normal there. The score relaxes this ceiling for the IT sector.
pb_ratio.watch_out: For a bank, a P/B under 1 is either a real bargain or the market telling you the loan book is worth less than reported.

ev_ebitda.label: EV/EBITDA
ev_ebitda.formula: (Market cap + debt − cash) ÷ earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation
ev_ebitda.plain: The price to buy the whole business including taking on its debts, divided by its rough operating cash profit. Think of it as the price a buyer would pay for the entire company rather than one share.

bands.note: Negative — the business is not generating operating profit

ev_ebitda.caveat: Fairer than P/E when comparing companies with different debt loads or tax rates, because it ignores both. Not used for banks and NBFCs — the score drops it for them.
ev_ebitda.watch_out: EBITDA ignores the cost of replacing worn-out equipment, so it flatters capital-hungry businesses.

peg_ratio.label: PEG Ratio
peg_ratio.formula: P/E ratio ÷ expected annual earnings growth rate (in %)
peg_ratio.plain: Puts the P/E in context of growth. A P/E of 30 is perfectly reasonable if profits are growing 30% a year — that is a PEG of 1.

bands.note: Negative — earnings or growth estimate is negative
Growth more than justifies the P/E

peg_ratio.caveat: Only as good as the growth estimate behind it, which is often missing entirely for Indian mid and small caps.
peg_ratio.watch_out: Useless for companies with lumpy or cyclical earnings — the growth figure swings wildly year to year.

dividend_yield.label: Dividend Yield
dividend_yield.formula: Annual dividend per share ÷ share price × 100
dividend_yield.plain: The cash the company pays you each year, as a percentage of what you paid for the share. Buy at ₹1,000 and collect ₹20 a year and the yield is 2%.
dividend_yield.caveat: A 0% yield is not bad — a fast-growing company reinvesting every rupee is often the better investment. Left out of the score for that reason.
dividend_yield.watch_out: A yield above 6% usually means the share price crashed, not that the dividend rose. Check whether the company can actually keep paying it.

trailing_eps.label: Trailing EPS
trailing_eps.formula: Net profit over the last 12 months ÷ number of shares
trailing_eps.plain: Each share's slice of last year's profit, in rupees. This is the 'E' underneath the P/E.
trailing_eps.caveat: The absolute level tells you nothing on its own — it depends entirely on how many shares exist. Only the direction matters, so it is not scored.
trailing_eps.watch_out: A share split or bonus issue cuts EPS overnight without anything changing about the business.

market_cap.label: Market Cap
market_cap.formula: Share price × total number of shares
market_cap.plain: What the market says the entire company is worth. It is the single most useful number for setting your expectations about volatility.
market_cap.ideal: Not better or worse — just different risk
market_cap.caveat: Rough India guide: large cap above ₹20,000 Cr (stable, heavily researched), mid cap ₹5,000–20,000 Cr, small cap below ₹5,000 Cr (can move 10% on no news at all). SEBI's official split is by rank, not rupees: top 100 companies are large cap, 101–250 mid cap, the rest small cap.
market_cap.watch_out: Small caps look cheap on every ratio far more often, because the risk of being wrong is higher.

roe.label: ROE
roe.plain: The return the company earns on the money its owners put in. ₹100 of shareholder money producing ₹18 of profit a year is an ROE of 18%. It is the closest thing to an interest rate on your share of the business.

bands.note: Weak — barely beats a fixed deposit

roe.caveat: Debt inflates ROE. Always read it alongside debt-to-equity — a 25% ROE built on heavy borrowing is riskier than an 18% ROE with none.
roe.watch_out: Companies that buy back lots of shares shrink their equity base, which lifts ROE without the business improving.

roce.label: ROCE
roce.plain: The same idea as ROE but measured on all the money the business uses — the owners' and the borrowed. This is the honest version, because it cannot be flattered by taking on debt.
roce.ideal: Above 15%, and it must comfortably beat the ~9–10% it costs to borrow in India

bands.note: Below the cost of borrowing — growth destroys value here

roce.caveat: ROCE above ROE usually signals very little debt. ROE far above ROCE means leverage, not the business, is doing the work. Not used for banks and NBFCs — their capital employed is mostly customer deposits, which makes even a healthy lender look unprofitable here.
roce.watch_out: If ROCE sits below the interest rate the company pays, every rupee it borrows to expand makes shareholders poorer.

profit_margin.label: Profit Margin
profit_margin.plain: Out of every ₹100 of sales, how much the company actually keeps as final profit after every cost, interest payment and tax.

bands.note: Thin — normal for retail and distribution

profit_margin.caveat: Wildly sector-dependent: 20%+ is normal for IT and branded FMCG, 5–10% for manufacturing, 1–3% for retail and distribution. A 2% margin supermarket is not a worse business than a 25% margin software firm — it just runs a different model.
profit_margin.watch_out: A sudden margin jump is often a one-off: an asset sale, an insurance payout, or a tax credit.

operating_margin.label: Operating Margin
operating_margin.plain: Profit from the core business before interest payments and tax muddy the picture. The cleanest read on whether the actual operation makes money.
operating_margin.ideal: Stable or rising, and comparable to industry peers

bands.note: The core operation is losing money

operating_margin.caveat: Compare it to the net margin. A wide gap between the two means interest costs are eating the profit — go and look at the debt.
operating_margin.watch_out: Falling operating margin while revenue grows means the company is buying growth with discounts.

debt_to_equity.label: Debt to Equity
debt_to_equity.plain: How many rupees the company has borrowed for every ₹1 of owner money. Shown here multiplied by 100, so a reading of 80 means 0.8x and 250 means 2.5x.
debt_to_equity.caveat: Ignore this entirely for banks and NBFCs — borrowing is their raw material and 5–10x is completely routine. The score drops it for those sectors.
debt_to_equity.watch_out: For every other kind of company this is the single best early warning of real trouble. Debt is what turns a bad year into bankruptcy.

free_cash_flow.label: Free Cash Flow
free_cash_flow.plain: The cash genuinely left over after running the business and paying for the new equipment it needs. This is the money actually available to pay down debt, pay dividends, or buy something.
free_cash_flow.caveat: Profit is an opinion shaped by accounting choices; cash is a fact. When the two disagree over several years, trust the cash. Not used for banks and NBFCs — a lender growing its loan book reports deeply negative cash flow precisely when business is good.
free_cash_flow.watch_out: Years of healthy reported profit alongside negative free cash flow is the classic accounting warning sign. A single negative year during a big expansion is normal.

net_cash.label: Net Cash Position
net_cash.plain: What is left if the company used all its cash to clear all its borrowings. Positive means it could pay off every lender tomorrow and still have money in the bank.
net_cash.ideal: Positive — net cash rather than net debt

bands.note: Net debt — normal, but read it with debt-to-equity
Net cash — a fortress balance sheet

net_cash.caveat: Gives the raw amounts behind the debt-to-equity ratio. A company with ₹5,000 Cr of debt and ₹6,000 Cr of cash has no debt problem at all.
net_cash.watch_out: Net debt is not automatically bad — cheap borrowing to fund a high-ROCE expansion creates value. It is net debt plus weak cash flow that kills.

cash_conversion.label: Earnings Quality
cash_conversion.full_name: Operating cash flow vs reported profit
cash_conversion.formula: Operating cash flow ÷ net profit (net profit derived from margin × revenue)
cash_conversion.plain: Checks whether the reported profit actually arrived as cash. A ratio near or above 1 means the profit is real money in the bank, not just an invoice someone has yet to pay.

bands.note: Operating cash flow is negative while profit is reported
Little of the reported profit is turning into cash
Some gap between profit and cash
Profit is backed by real cash

cash_conversion.caveat: Can swing around in a single year as customers pay early or late. Worth checking over several years before drawing conclusions.
cash_conversion.watch_out: Profit rising while operating cash flow stays flat means sales are being booked but not collected. Question the earnings.

revenue_growth.label: Revenue Growth
revenue_growth.plain: How much the company's sales grew compared with last year. Sales are the top line — everything else is a slice of it.

bands.note: Stagnant — barely keeping up with inflation

revenue_growth.caveat: Revenue is much harder to massage than profit, so trust this more than earnings growth when the two disagree.
revenue_growth.watch_out: Growth bought through acquisitions is not the same as the existing business growing. Check whether the company bought its way there.

earnings_growth.label: Earnings Growth
earnings_growth.plain: How much profit grew compared with last year. Ideally it grows faster than revenue, which means each rupee of sales is becoming more profitable.
earnings_growth.ideal: Positive and ideally faster than revenue growth

bands.note: Very strong — verify it is not a one-off

earnings_growth.caveat: The lumpiest number on this page. A single asset sale, write-off or tax change can make it meaningless — always check three to five years.
earnings_growth.watch_out: Earnings growing much faster than revenue year after year cannot continue forever; margins have a ceiling.

revenue_consistency.label: Revenue Consistency
revenue_consistency.formula: Share of years in which revenue rose, across the annual history available
revenue_consistency.plain: Out of the last few years, how often sales actually went up. Steady year-after-year growth is far more valuable than one spectacular year surrounded by flat ones.
revenue_consistency.caveat: Computed from the annual figures in the Revenue & Profit Trend chart below, so it only covers the years Yahoo Finance supplies — usually four.
revenue_consistency.watch_out: Cyclical businesses (metals, chemicals, real estate) will always look inconsistent here. That is the nature of the sector, not a defect.

promoter_holding.label: Promoter Holding
promoter_holding.formula: Shares held by founders or the parent company ÷ total shares × 100
promoter_holding.plain: How much of the company the founders or parent still own. High promoter holding means the people running it lose money alongside you when they get it wrong.
promoter_holding.ideal: Above 50% is strong skin in the game; 30–50% is fine

bands.note: Low — common in professionally run and older listed companies
Very high — little free float, so the price can be volatile

promoter_holding.caveat: This figure comes from Yahoo Finance's 'insider holding' field, which is an imperfect proxy for the Indian promoter-holding disclosure. Verify it on the NSE site before relying on it.
promoter_holding.watch_out: The direction matters far more than the level. Steady promoter selling quarter after quarter, or a high percentage that turns out to be pledged against loans, is the real red flag.

how_it_works: Four pillars — Valuation, Profitability, Balance sheet, Growth & ownership — worth 25 points each, for a total of 100.
Each metric is graded against the bands listed above: good scores its full weight, neutral 55%, bad 10%.
Metrics with no data are excluded and the pillar rescales to 25, so a stock with patchy data is not silently punished.
Banks and NBFCs skip EV/EBITDA and debt-to-equity, because borrowing is their business rather than a risk. IT companies get a relaxed price-to-book ceiling, since they own few physical assets.
The confidence label tells you how many of the metrics actually had data. A low-confidence score is a provisional reading, not a verdict.
scoring.limits: This score only measures what is in these numbers. It knows nothing about management quality, competition, pending litigation, pledged promoter shares, related-party transactions, or whether today's price is sensible against the next five years. It is a reading aid to help you learn what the metrics mean — not a recommendation, and not a substitute for reading the company's own filings.
